final_recommendation: The room converged on a Protocol of Amendment to be signed December 10th, containing facility-level labor enforcement with a trilateral inspection mechanism, automatic 90-day cure triggers upon non-compliance findings, sector-specific trade suspensions, and explicit scope limitation to the labor chapter only. Congressional Democrats committed to third-week January ratification vote contingent on final text matching agreed terms.
minority_objections: Mexico initially resisted automatic suspension triggers as sovereignty infringement, requiring negotiation to accept 90-day cure period with remediation control
Business lobby expressed concern about timeline uncertainty and potential for last-minute text changes derailing January mobilization
key_conflicts: Automatic enforcement triggers vs. Mexican sovereignty concerns over unilateral U.S. veto power
Congressional demand for transparent facility-level reporting vs. Mexico's resistance to public naming-and-shaming
Tension between enforcement credibility (immediate consequences) and procedural fairness (cure periods)
Inspector independence and tie-breaking authority in trilateral verification mechanism
key_concessions: Mexico accepted facility-level verification and sector-specific suspension in exchange for 90-day cure period and confidentiality on facility names
U.S. Congress accepted 90-day cure window instead of immediate tariff snapback in exchange for automatic trigger mechanism
Canada accepted labor enforcement amendment in exchange for explicit scope limitation protecting dairy and Chapter 19
All parties accepted neutral third inspector as tie-breaker with monthly aggregate reporting to Congress
red_lines: Mexico: no blanket tariff snapback or public facility naming; sovereignty over remediation process during cure period
U.S. Congress: automatic trigger without Mexican veto; no softening of 'consider suspension' language; explicit scope limitation in Protocol text itself
Canada: amendment must not reopen dairy concessions or Chapter 19; labor-only modification
Business lobby: no delays beyond third-week January vote; December 10th text must be final
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation capacity: no discussion of whether Mexico can actually staff/fund trilateral inspections at scale
Neutral inspector selection process and potential for deadlock over who qualifies as 'neutral'
What happens if multiple sectors simultaneously fail benchmarks—resource constraints on enforcement
Political risk that Mexican domestic opposition to 'occupation-style' monitoring undermines compliance even with sovereignty protections
Timeline risk: 10 p.m. same-day signing deadline creates pressure for errors in final text
No discussion of what 'sector-specific suspension' means operationally—which products, how targeted
downstream_risk_variables: Whether December 10th Protocol text precisely matches verbal agreements or contains ambiguities that reignite disputes
Mexico's actual compliance during first 90-day cycles—whether cure periods become routine delays
Congressional reaction if early enforcement cases reveal weaknesses in neutral inspector independence
Canadian domestic backlash if opposition frames labor amendment as precedent for reopening other chapters
Business community response if January vote slips due to text discrepancies or last-minute objections
Media narrative sustainability if enforcement produces few visible results in first year
uncertainty_notes: Final Protocol language not yet reviewed by all parties; operational details of neutral inspector selection, facility benchmark definitions, and sector-specific suspension scope remain unspecified; no contingency plan if December 10th signing deadline is missed; unclear whether monthly reporting cadence provides sufficient early-warning for compliance issues.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Dominated entire meeting—Congressman's opening 'we don't have the votes' and repeated 'deal's dead on arrival' warnings drove every compromise; ratification_prospects variable climbed from 38→77 as mechanism was built
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Central driver throughout—union's facility-level benchmarks demand, Congressman's 'quarterly reporting isn't enforcement' rejection, and insistence on automatic triggers shaped the entire Protocol structure
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Present and influential but not dominant—business secured January timeline commitment and certainty language, but deferred to labor enforcement mechanics; conditioned support rather than driving room direction
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Genuine concern developed across R1-R5—Canada repeatedly demanded explicit scope limitation to protect dairy/Chapter 19, made it ratification condition, but didn't drive overall enforcement design
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Core tension throughout—Mexico's 'sovereignty issue we can't swallow' on tariff snapback, resistance to public facility naming, and insistence on remediation control forced major mechanism redesigns (90-day cure, confidentiality protections)
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Mentioned but not driving—media actor asked clarifying questions about narrative and timelines, but didn't shape substantive enforcement mechanics; room focused on Congressional/labor/Mexico triangle
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Implicit assumption rather than explicit driver—room treated amendment as necessary for ratification but focused on mechanism design rather than debating whether stability required reopening; Canada's scope-limitation concern touched this but wasn't central theme
